newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin not disturbed by higher rates.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin not disturbed by higher rates.

text.p: Rising Canadian interest rates will not interfere with the government's plans to pay off the deficit, Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Wednesday.
"That's the purpose of the contingency reserve," Martin said after a caucus meeting, referring to the C$2.5 billion built in to the budget in case economic assumptions are off.
"All I'm going to tell you is that when we set our fiscal track, there are a lot of variables out there and we are going to cover them the best we could," Martin said.

The Bank of Canada hiked interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month, the first rise in years. Martin and his Liberal government have taken credit for Canada's low interest rates and benefited from lower rates to pay off the deficit.

"The government's largest single expense item is our interest rates. Very clearly if you're going to have a deficit reduction program, the most successful way to do it was to get interest rates down and that requires credibility," Martin said. "I think we were successful in doing that."

He said that despite the recent hike in interest rates and market expectations that rates would continue to inch up, it was significant that Canada's short-term rates were still lower than in the United States.

Canada's once overwhelming deficit was well under control, Martin said. He repeated that the final budget deficit numbers for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1996, would show a deficit under C$16 billion.
That amount is even lower than the government's C$17 billion target for the current fiscal year, but Martin said he would not revise his targets until a budget update this autumn.
